currentContext.strengths: Captive renewable power: own wind farms met 56% of total power requirement in FY 2025-26 (PY: 50%), and the Company states power cost fell despite a tariff increase by Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited and higher consumption.|Mix shift into value-added products: "Over the last five years, the share of value-added products has increased from 12% to 40%."|Product flexibility: "the Company's focus on producing a flexible and diversified range of products helped protect its sales volumes during this sluggish period" while other Indian spinning mills ran at lower capacities.|Forward integration and synergy between spinning and fabric capacities, stated to enable a wide range of textile products with quick turnaround times.|Traceability of the entire production process plus product enhancement through technology advancement and customer-centricity, cited as supporting export volumes.|Long-standing export relationship with M/s. Asahi Kasei Advance Corporation, Japan, thanked by the Directors for continued support in promoting exports to Japan.|"A Grade" in Social Audit Compliance, with leading domestic and international brands increasingly approaching the Company for sourcing yarn and fabric.|Global cotton sourcing flexibility: the Company shifted focus to value-added counts and imported higher-quality cotton when prices were reasonable, procuring diversified varieties from across the globe.|ERP system developed by associate M/s. Ramco Systems Limited installed for online monitoring of all functions and MIS-based internal control.|Group affiliation evidenced by three associate holdings - The Ramco Cements Limited, Ramco Industries Limited and Ramco Systems Limited - and a shared board with those companies.
currentContext.strategies: Shift the sales mix towards more value-added counts and away from commodity counts - Mercerized Yarn, Melange Yarn, Core Yarn, Elitwist, Gassing, High Twist - with the stated result that the share of value-added products rose from 12% to 40% over the last five years.|Buy cotton opportunistically and globally: import higher-quality cotton when prices are at reasonable levels and procure diversified varieties from across the globe, so as to offer competitively priced yarn.|Modernise the spinning mills and forward-integrate through fabric manufacturing and processing facilities, to drive top-line growth and protect margins.|Exploit the synergy between the Company's spinning and fabric capacities to offer a wide range of textile products with quick turnaround times.|Strengthen infrastructure to manufacture a flexible and diversified product range, and co-develop innovative products with customers, to defend capacity utilisation and export sales volumes through weak demand.|Compete on quality and traceability rather than price alone: product enhancement through technology advancement, traceability of the entire production process, continuous customer-centricity, continuous monitoring of process parameters and robust system controls.|Sustainable manufacturing as a positioning plank - water reuse, zero-liquid-discharge systems and bio-treatment of wastewater for recycling - stated as positioning the Company among the leading textile companies globally.|Maximise self-generated renewable power for captive consumption (own wind farms) to contain power cost against rising grid tariffs.|Convert brand interest into business: leverage the "A Grade" in Social Audit Compliance as leading domestic and international brands increasingly approach the Company for sourcing yarn and fabric.|Dividend is the only capital-return channel disclosed in this bundle, and it is put to members as an ordinary resolution at the 90th AGM (Video Conferencing / OAVM, 11:00 A.M., Friday 28th August 2026) for the year ended 31st March 2026, payable to shareholders on the Register of Members and Register of Beneficial Owners as on 21st August 2026. [BACK-FILLED FROM THE SIBLING PROFILE / STRATEGY BUNDLE, not present in this routed text: the Company states the dividend is declared out of Free Reserves in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013 and its 'Dividend Distribution Policy' (published on its website); that under the Income Tax Act, 2025 dividend is taxable in shareholders' hands and will be paid after deducting applicable TDS; that the recommended rate is unchanged year on year; that it has opted to pay tax under Section 115BAA; and that FY26 modernisation capex was 'funded from internal accruals and loan from Banks', with additional term loan borrowings and enhanced fabric capacity raising finance cost.] No buyback, no debt-reduction target, no credit rating, no dividend payout-ratio policy and no formal capital-allocation framework is disclosed anywhere in this bundle.|Sustainable manufacturing initiatives stated as including water reuse, zero-liquid-discharge (ZLD) systems and bio-treatment of wastewater for recycling - management frames these as reinforcing its environmental commitment and positioning it among the leading textile companies globally.|Captive renewable power: windmills of 35.15 MW installed capacity for captive consumption; the wind farm generated 696 Lakhs Kwh in FY 2025-26 against 573 Lakhs Kwh in the previous year, and ALL units generated were adjusted for captive consumption at the Company's Spinning / Fabric Division.|Renewable share of own consumption rose to 56% of total power requirement in FY 2025-26 from 50% in the previous year - the single most trackable environmental KPI the Company discloses.|Social: the Company has secured an "A Grade" in Social Audit Compliance, which it links to leading domestic and international brands increasingly approaching it for sourcing yarn and fabric.|Traceability of the entire production process is cited as part of the Company's product-enhancement and export proposition - relevant to cotton-origin and supply-chain-transparency requirements of global brands.|Governance-adjacent: a Vigil Mechanism / Whistle Blower Policy is in place with Whistle Blower Drop Boxes, dedicated e-mail addresses accessible only by a Corporate Ombudsman, confidentiality and anonymity protection, and complainant access to the Chairman of the Audit Committee (back-filled from the sibling profile bundle - the Directors'-Report text routed here is cut before this item).
currentContext.expansion: The only expansion activity the Company describes for FY 2025-26 is modernisation rather than greenfield capacity: under the heading 'MODERNISATION / EXPANSION' it states it invested $ 35.09 Crores (rupee glyph is mojibake in the source) in modernising Comber Machine, Carding Machine, Sectional Warping Machine, Raising Machine etc., funded from internal accruals and loan from Banks. Separately, the finance-cost commentary attributes higher borrowing to 'Additional working capital requirements, enhanced Fabric capacity and additional term loan borrowings', which is the only reference to fabric capacity having been enhanced during the year - no size, cost or commissioning date is attached to it. The standing asset base is described as a Fabric Unit 'operating with 328 Looms and finishing capacity capable of producing 50,000 meters of finished fabrics per day', and windmills 'with installed capacity of 35.15 MW for its captive power consumption'. Looking forward, the Company says only that 'modernization of spinning mills and forward integration through the establishment of fabric manufacturing and processing facilities are expected to drive top-line growth and protect margins during the current year' and that spinning-fabric synergies should let it offer a wide range of textile products with quick turnaround times. NO named future project, no announced capacity addition, no capex budget for the year ahead and no commissioning or ramp timeline is disclosed anywhere in this bundle; spinning capacity (spindleage) is never stated in any year.
currentContext.mdna: Cotton-to-yarn spread is the central margin driver: despite some correction in cotton prices, the decline in yarn prices was significantly sharper, producing a wider disparity that adversely affected the margins of yarn spinners across India.|Demand: sluggish market demand for cotton yarn plus geopolitical challenges forced many Indian spinning mills to operate at lower capacities, several reducing production on substantial losses in yarn manufacturing.|Global supply: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service data cited for global cotton production in the 2026-27 season expected to decline by 5%, on lower production projections for Australia, Brazil, China, Pakistan, Turkey and the United States.|Global demand: global cotton consumption projected to grow by 1.33%, on larger global cotton supplies, replenishment of inventories across the textile and apparel supply chain and prospects for global economic growth.|Indian crop: cotton production in season 2024-25 was 313 lakh bales (170 kg each) vs 327 lakh bales, a 4% decline on reduced acreage; CAI estimated 305 lakh bales for 2025-26 but revised arrivals up to 320 lakh bales.|Policy support on the input side: CCI procured 91 lakh bales in season 2025-26 (as on 05-02-2026) and raised MSP for medium and long staple cotton by 8%; the Government of India exempted import duty on cotton from 30-09-2025 to 31-12-2025 to improve domestic raw-cotton availability, stabilise prices and reduce input costs.|Trade access: the India-UK Free Trade Agreement signed in May 2025 has opened new export opportunities for the textile industry, and the India-Europe Free Trade Agreement signed in January 2026 is described as a strategic breakthrough in India's global trade engagement.|Export logistics as a cost/lead-time drag: the Red Sea crisis significantly impacted exports, resulting in higher freight and insurance costs along with shipping delays.|Mix as the margin lever: strengthening the portfolio with value-added and customised counts is expected to help mitigate the impact of falling demand for commodity counts.|Cost lever: rising power tariff from Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited offset by higher captive wind consumption (56% of total power requirement vs 50%), better wind velocity and favourable weather.|Price reference band cited by management: international cotton traded in a range of 74.05 to 78.81 US cents per LB against domestic cotton at 78.75 to 81.50 US cents per LB - i.e. domestic cotton at a premium to international.|Customer pull: quality of fabric well accepted in domestic and export markets, generating numerous enquiries from leading brands across the globe for the supply of processed fabric.

risks.risk: Cotton-to-yarn spread compression - the core structural risk of a commodity spinner
risks.note: Management states that despite some correction in cotton prices, the decline in yarn prices was significantly sharper, 'resulting in a wider disparity that adversely affected the margins of yarn spinners across India'. The Company buys a crop and sells a commodity, and the two prices moved apart against it; management adds that 'Volatility in cotton prices continues, with both cotton and yarn prices experiencing wide fluctuations', so the exposure is stated to be live, not resolved.

risks.risk: Weak end-demand for cotton yarn, forcing industry-wide under-utilisation
risks.note: 'Due to geopolitical challenges and sluggish market demand for cotton yarn, spinning mills faced severe pressure on margins. This situation forced many spinning mills across India to operate at lower capacities, with several mills reducing production due to substantial losses in yarn manufacturing.' The Company says its flexible and diversified product range protected its own sales volumes, but the demand backdrop is industry-wide and outside its control.

risks.risk: Falling demand specifically for commodity counts, and a value-added mix that shrank in absolute volume
risks.note: Management identifies 'falling demand for commodity counts' as the thing the value-added strategy must mitigate - yet the value-added leg itself contracted this year: sales volume of Elitwist, Gassing, High Twist, Melange, Core Yarn and Mercerized Yarn 'decreased to 2,800 tonnes during FY 2025-26 from 3,255 tonnes in the previous year'. The stated mitigant weakened in the same period the risk was flagged.

'the Red Sea crisis significantly impacted exports, resulting in higher freight and insurance costs, along with shipping delays.' Exports are a material channel for both yarn (including merchant exports) and fabric, so a shipping-route disruption hits landed cost and lead time simultaneously.

risks.risk: Raw-material availability and policy dependence on the cotton crop
risks.note: Indian cotton production fell 4% to 313 lakh bales in season 2024-25 on reduced acreage; CAI initially estimated only 305 lakh bales for 2025-26 (arrivals later revised up to 320 lakh bales); CCI procured 91 lakh bales and MSP for medium and long staple cotton was raised 8%, which supports the input price the Company pays. Relief came from a temporary policy action - the Government exempted import duty on cotton only from 30-09-2025 to 31-12-2025 - so the input-cost benefit is time-limited by construction. Looking ahead, USDA FAS data cited by management has global cotton production for 2026-27 declining 5%.

risks.risk: Grid power tariff inflation, mitigated by but also dependent on captive wind
risks.note: Power tariff was increased by Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited and consumption rose, yet power cost fell because own wind farms met 56% of total requirement (PY 50%). Management attributes the improvement to 'better wind velocity, favourable weather conditions' - i.e. a majority of the Company's power economics now rides on weather-dependent generation, and a poor wind year reverses the benefit.

risks.risk: Financing cost and leverage on a loss-making base
risks.note: Finance cost rose year on year, attributed by management to 'Additional working capital requirements, enhanced Fabric capacity and additional term loan borrowings'. The Company is simultaneously funding modernisation from internal accruals and bank loans while reporting no current tax liability because it is not liable to pay income tax for the year - a combination that makes debt service the binding constraint. (Rupee amounts and leverage ratios deliberately not reproduced here.)

risks.risk: Customer and channel concentration in exports
risks.note: The only export counterparty named anywhere in the bundle is 'M/s. Asahi Kasei Advance Corporation, Japan', thanked by the Directors 'for their continued support and efforts towards promoting exports to Japan'. The bundle gives no customer-concentration table, so the degree of dependence cannot be quantified - but a single named promoter of a whole export geography is a structural exposure worth tracking.

Every disclosed revenue-generating activity - yarn, fabric, captive wind power - sits on cotton textiles in one value chain, with no unrelated diversification. The only earnings source outside textiles disclosed in the bundle is dividend income from the three associate holdings (The Ramco Cements, Ramco Industries, Ramco Systems), which is a portfolio exposure rather than an operating hedge.

themes.title: Textiles - apparel/home-textile exports + synthetics
themes.need: India textiles ride three tailwinds at once: China+1 sourcing shifts, the India-UK FTA (signed) + India-EU FTA (advancing), and US tariff normalization - favouring apparel exporters (GOKEX/PGIL/PDSL) and US-heavy home-textile names (WELSPUNLIV/HIMATSEIDE). A second leg = value-added synthetics/recycling (FILATEX, SANATHAN, CENTENKA, GANECOS) and cotton-yarn spread recovery (VTL/NITINSPIN/SPORTKING) plus branded apparel (PAGEIND, ARVIND, RAYMONDLSL).
themes.driver: FTA implementation + US-India trade-deal clarity; festive/wedding demand; cotton-yarn spread; anti-dumping rulings.

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Yarn:** Cotton Yarn, Elitwist, Gassing, High Twist, Melange Yarn, Core Yarn, Mercerized Yarn
- **Fabric:** Finished / processed fabric
- **Power:** Captive wind power (windmill division)

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- Domestic Indian yarn and fabric market
- Export markets (cotton yarn, including merchant exports)
- Japan (exports promoted through M/s. Asahi Kasei Advance Corporation, Japan)
- Leading domestic and international brands sourcing yarn and fabric
- Captive internal consumption (windmill output adjusted at the Company's Spinning / Fabric Division)

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Cotton-to-yarn spread is the central margin driver: despite some correction in cotton prices, the decline in yarn prices was significantly sharper, producing a wider disparity that adversely affected the margins of yarn spinners across India.
- Demand: sluggish market demand for cotton yarn plus geopolitical challenges forced many Indian spinning mills to operate at lower capacities, several reducing production on substantial losses in yarn manufacturing.
- Global supply: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service data cited for global cotton production in the 2026-27 season expected to decline by 5%, on lower production projections for Australia, Brazil, China, Pakistan, Turkey and the United States.
- Global demand: global cotton consumption projected to grow by 1.33%, on larger global cotton supplies, replenishment of inventories across the textile and apparel supply chain and prospects for global economic growth.
- Indian crop: cotton production in season 2024-25 was 313 lakh bales (170 kg each) vs 327 lakh bales, a 4% decline on reduced acreage; CAI estimated 305 lakh bales for 2025-26 but revised arrivals up to 320 lakh bales.
- Policy support on the input side: CCI procured 91 lakh bales in season 2025-26 (as on 05-02-2026) and raised MSP for medium and long staple cotton by 8%; the Government of India exempted import duty on cotton from 30-09-2025 to 31-12-2025 to improve domestic raw-cotton availability, stabilise prices and reduce input costs.
- Trade access: the India-UK Free Trade Agreement signed in May 2025 has opened new export opportunities for the textile industry, and the India-Europe Free Trade Agreement signed in January 2026 is described as a strategic breakthrough in India's global trade engagement.
- Export logistics as a cost/lead-time drag: the Red Sea crisis significantly impacted exports, resulting in higher freight and insurance costs along with shipping delays.
- Mix as the margin lever: strengthening the portfolio with value-added and customised counts is expected to help mitigate the impact of falling demand for commodity counts.
- Cost lever: rising power tariff from Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited offset by higher captive wind consumption (56% of total power requirement vs 50%), better wind velocity and favourable weather.
- Price reference band cited by management: international cotton traded in a range of 74.05 to 78.81 US cents per LB against domestic cotton at 78.75 to 81.50 US cents per LB - i.e. domestic cotton at a premium to international.
- Customer pull: quality of fabric well accepted in domestic and export markets, generating numerous enquiries from leading brands across the globe for the supply of processed fabric.

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Shift the sales mix towards more value-added counts and away from commodity counts - Mercerized Yarn, Melange Yarn, Core Yarn, Elitwist, Gassing, High Twist - with the stated result that the share of value-added products rose from 12% to 40% over the last five years.
- Buy cotton opportunistically and globally: import higher-quality cotton when prices are at reasonable levels and procure diversified varieties from across the globe, so as to offer competitively priced yarn.
- Modernise the spinning mills and forward-integrate through fabric manufacturing and processing facilities, to drive top-line growth and protect margins.
- Exploit the synergy between the Company's spinning and fabric capacities to offer a wide range of textile products with quick turnaround times.
- Strengthen infrastructure to manufacture a flexible and diversified product range, and co-develop innovative products with customers, to defend capacity utilisation and export sales volumes through weak demand.
- Compete on quality and traceability rather than price alone: product enhancement through technology advancement, traceability of the entire production process, continuous customer-centricity, continuous monitoring of process parameters and robust system controls.
- Sustainable manufacturing as a positioning plank - water reuse, zero-liquid-discharge systems and bio-treatment of wastewater for recycling - stated as positioning the Company among the leading textile companies globally.
- Maximise self-generated renewable power for captive consumption (own wind farms) to contain power cost against rising grid tariffs.
- Convert brand interest into business: leverage the "A Grade" in Social Audit Compliance as leading domestic and international brands increasingly approach the Company for sourcing yarn and fabric.
- Dividend is the only capital-return channel disclosed in this bundle, and it is put to members as an ordinary resolution at the 90th AGM (Video Conferencing / OAVM, 11:00 A.M., Friday 28th August 2026) for the year ended 31st March 2026, payable to shareholders on the Register of Members and Register of Beneficial Owners as on 21st August 2026. [BACK-FILLED FROM THE SIBLING PROFILE / STRATEGY BUNDLE, not present in this routed text: the Company states the dividend is declared out of Free Reserves in accordance with the Companies Act, 2013 and its 'Dividend Distribution Policy' (published on its website); that under the Income Tax Act, 2025 dividend is taxable in shareholders' hands and will be paid after deducting applicable TDS; that the recommended rate is unchanged year on year; that it has opted to pay tax under Section 115BAA; and that FY26 modernisation capex was 'funded from internal accruals and loan from Banks', with additional term loan borrowings and enhanced fabric capacity raising finance cost.] No buyback, no debt-reduction target, no credit rating, no dividend payout-ratio policy and no formal capital-allocation framework is disclosed anywhere in this bundle.
- Sustainable manufacturing initiatives stated as including water reuse, zero-liquid-discharge (ZLD) systems and bio-treatment of wastewater for recycling - management frames these as reinforcing its environmental commitment and positioning it among the leading textile companies globally.
- Captive renewable power: windmills of 35.15 MW installed capacity for captive consumption; the wind farm generated 696 Lakhs Kwh in FY 2025-26 against 573 Lakhs Kwh in the previous year, and ALL units generated were adjusted for captive consumption at the Company's Spinning / Fabric Division.
- Renewable share of own consumption rose to 56% of total power requirement in FY 2025-26 from 50% in the previous year - the single most trackable environmental KPI the Company discloses.
- Social: the Company has secured an "A Grade" in Social Audit Compliance, which it links to leading domestic and international brands increasingly approaching it for sourcing yarn and fabric.
- Traceability of the entire production process is cited as part of the Company's product-enhancement and export proposition - relevant to cotton-origin and supply-chain-transparency requirements of global brands.
- Governance-adjacent: a Vigil Mechanism / Whistle Blower Policy is in place with Whistle Blower Drop Boxes, dedicated e-mail addresses accessible only by a Corporate Ombudsman, confidentiality and anonymity protection, and complainant access to the Chairman of the Audit Committee (back-filled from the sibling profile bundle - the Directors'-Report text routed here is cut before this item).

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The only expansion activity the Company describes for FY 2025-26 is modernisation rather than greenfield capacity: under the heading 'MODERNISATION / EXPANSION' it states it invested $ 35.09 Crores (rupee glyph is mojibake in the source) in modernising Comber Machine, Carding Machine, Sectional Warping Machine, Raising Machine etc., funded from internal accruals and loan from Banks. Separately, the finance-cost commentary attributes higher borrowing to 'Additional working capital requirements, enhanced Fabric capacity and additional term loan borrowings', which is the only reference to fabric capacity having been enhanced during the year - no size, cost or commissioning date is attached to it. The standing asset base is described as a Fabric Unit 'operating with 328 Looms and finishing capacity capable of producing 50,000 meters of finished fabrics per day', and windmills 'with installed capacity of 35.15 MW for its captive power consumption'. Looking forward, the Company says only that 'modernization of spinning mills and forward integration through the establishment of fabric manufacturing and processing facilities are expected to drive top-line growth and protect margins during the current year' and that spinning-fabric synergies should let it offer a wide range of textile products with quick turnaround times. NO named future project, no announced capacity addition, no capex budget for the year ahead and no commissioning or ramp timeline is disclosed anywhere in this bundle; spinning capacity (spindleage) is never stated in any year.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Captive renewable power: own wind farms met 56% of total power requirement in FY 2025-26 (PY: 50%), and the Company states power cost fell despite a tariff increase by Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited and higher consumption.
- Mix shift into value-added products: "Over the last five years, the share of value-added products has increased from 12% to 40%."
- Product flexibility: "the Company's focus on producing a flexible and diversified range of products helped protect its sales volumes during this sluggish period" while other Indian spinning mills ran at lower capacities.
- Forward integration and synergy between spinning and fabric capacities, stated to enable a wide range of textile products with quick turnaround times.
- Traceability of the entire production process plus product enhancement through technology advancement and customer-centricity, cited as supporting export volumes.
- Long-standing export relationship with M/s. Asahi Kasei Advance Corporation, Japan, thanked by the Directors for continued support in promoting exports to Japan.
- "A Grade" in Social Audit Compliance, with leading domestic and international brands increasingly approaching the Company for sourcing yarn and fabric.
- Global cotton sourcing flexibility: the Company shifted focus to value-added counts and imported higher-quality cotton when prices were reasonable, procuring diversified varieties from across the globe.
- ERP system developed by associate M/s. Ramco Systems Limited installed for online monitoring of all functions and MIS-based internal control.
- Group affiliation evidenced by three associate holdings - The Ramco Cements Limited, Ramco Industries Limited and Ramco Systems Limited - and a shared board with those companies.

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Cotton-to-yarn spread compression - the core structural risk of a commodity spinner — Management states that despite some correction in cotton prices, the decline in yarn prices was significantly sharper, 'resulting in a wider disparity that adversely affected the margins of yarn spinners across India'. The Company buys a crop and sells a commodity, and the two prices moved apart against it; management adds that 'Volatility in cotton prices continues, with both cotton and yarn prices experiencing wide fluctuations', so the exposure is stated to be live, not resolved.
- Weak end-demand for cotton yarn, forcing industry-wide under-utilisation — 'Due to geopolitical challenges and sluggish market demand for cotton yarn, spinning mills faced severe pressure on margins. This situation forced many spinning mills across India to operate at lower capacities, with several mills reducing production due to substantial losses in yarn manufacturing.' The Company says its flexible and diversified product range protected its own sales volumes, but the demand backdrop is industry-wide and outside its control.
- Falling demand specifically for commodity counts, and a value-added mix that shrank in absolute volume — Management identifies 'falling demand for commodity counts' as the thing the value-added strategy must mitigate - yet the value-added leg itself contracted this year: sales volume of Elitwist, Gassing, High Twist, Melange, Core Yarn and Mercerized Yarn 'decreased to 2,800 tonnes during FY 2025-26 from 3,255 tonnes in the previous year'. The stated mitigant weakened in the same period the risk was flagged.
- Export logistics and freight disruption — 'the Red Sea crisis significantly impacted exports, resulting in higher freight and insurance costs, along with shipping delays.' Exports are a material channel for both yarn (including merchant exports) and fabric, so a shipping-route disruption hits landed cost and lead time simultaneously.
- Raw-material availability and policy dependence on the cotton crop — Indian cotton production fell 4% to 313 lakh bales in season 2024-25 on reduced acreage; CAI initially estimated only 305 lakh bales for 2025-26 (arrivals later revised up to 320 lakh bales); CCI procured 91 lakh bales and MSP for medium and long staple cotton was raised 8%, which supports the input price the Company pays. Relief came from a temporary policy action - the Government exempted import duty on cotton only from 30-09-2025 to 31-12-2025 - so the input-cost benefit is time-limited by construction. Looking ahead, USDA FAS data cited by management has global cotton production for 2026-27 declining 5%.
- Grid power tariff inflation, mitigated by but also dependent on captive wind — Power tariff was increased by Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited and consumption rose, yet power cost fell because own wind farms met 56% of total requirement (PY 50%). Management attributes the improvement to 'better wind velocity, favourable weather conditions' - i.e. a majority of the Company's power economics now rides on weather-dependent generation, and a poor wind year reverses the benefit.
- Financing cost and leverage on a loss-making base — Finance cost rose year on year, attributed by management to 'Additional working capital requirements, enhanced Fabric capacity and additional term loan borrowings'. The Company is simultaneously funding modernisation from internal accruals and bank loans while reporting no current tax liability because it is not liable to pay income tax for the year - a combination that makes debt service the binding constraint. (Rupee amounts and leverage ratios deliberately not reproduced here.)
- Customer and channel concentration in exports — The only export counterparty named anywhere in the bundle is 'M/s. Asahi Kasei Advance Corporation, Japan', thanked by the Directors 'for their continued support and efforts towards promoting exports to Japan'. The bundle gives no customer-concentration table, so the degree of dependence cannot be quantified - but a single named promoter of a whole export geography is a structural exposure worth tracking.
- Single-activity, single-crop concentration — Every disclosed revenue-generating activity - yarn, fabric, captive wind power - sits on cotton textiles in one value chain, with no unrelated diversification. The only earnings source outside textiles disclosed in the bundle is dividend income from the three associate holdings (The Ramco Cements, Ramco Industries, Ramco Systems), which is a portfolio exposure rather than an operating hedge.
